meta_title: The First Sixty Days: Acclimating a Freshly Imported Aroid
meta_description: A field-tested protocol for nursing imported rare aroids back to health — sphagnum chambers, humidity ramps, and patient root recovery.
title: The First Sixty Days: Acclimating a Freshly Imported Aroid
deck: What happens between the customs box and a settled, growing plant is the part nobody photographs.
intro: The box arrives on a Tuesday, usually, because someone in Florida or Long Beach has timed the inspection right. You cut the tape and the smell hits first — wet kraft paper, a faint vinegar tang from stressed tissue, the green-mineral note of fresh sphagnum. Inside, swaddled in damp moss and newsprint, are three bare-root cuttings of _Anthurium papillilaminum_, a single-node _Philodendron spiritus-sancti_, and a leafless rhizome chunk that was sold to you as _Anthurium dressleri_ and may or may not be. You have maybe twenty minutes of adrenaline before the responsible part of your brain catches up.

Everyone obsesses over the purchase. The acclimation is where collectors actually lose plants. The first sixty days after import — when the roots are compromised, the leaves are running on stored sugar, and the plant is trying to read a new climate through closed stomata — decide whether you keep a $400 cutting or compost it in March. What follows is the protocol I've settled on after a decade of imports from Ecuador, Indonesia, and Thailand, and the reasoning behind each step.
pull_quote: An imported aroid is not a sick plant. It is a healthy plant that has been asked to do something biologically absurd.
body_image_caption: A papillilaminum cutting, day nine, in long-fiber sphagnum.

sections.heading: Triage on the kitchen counter
paragraphs: Unbox over a clean towel, not the sink. You want to see what falls out. Photograph everything before you touch it — for the seller, for insurance, and for your own records when you're trying to remember six weeks later whether that necrotic spot was there on arrival. Note the smell. Sour or fishy means anaerobic rot somewhere in the packaging, and you'll need to find it.

Unwrap each plant individually and lay them out. Rinse the roots and rhizome in tepid water — not cold, which shocks tropical tissue that's been sitting at 75°F in a box. I use a weak hydrogen peroxide rinse (one part 3% peroxide to four parts water) only on cuttings with visible rot or cut surfaces; on intact healthy roots it's unnecessary and arguably damaging to the beneficial microbiome you actually want to preserve.

Now assess. A freshly imported _Philodendron_ cutting with a firm petiole stub, a plump node, and even one aerial root is in good shape regardless of how shabby the leaf looks. An _Anthurium_ with mushy basal tissue is a different conversation: cut back to clean white or pale green cross-section, dust with cinnamon or sulfur if you like (I do, mostly out of habit), and accept that you're now propagating a smaller plant than you paid for. Better to know on day one.

sections.heading: Why sphagnum, and which sphagnum
paragraphs: Long-fiber sphagnum is the acclimation medium for almost any imported aroid because it does three things at once: holds moisture without going anaerobic if packed loosely, buffers humidity around the root zone, and lets you see exactly what the roots are doing. Chilean sphagnum (the AAA or 5-star grades from New Zealand and Chile) has the long, springy fibers you want. The compressed bricks of orchid-grade moss from Indonesia are cheaper and finer; they pack denser and rot quicker. For acclimation, spend the money.

Soak the moss in rainwater or RO water for at least an hour, then squeeze it out until it's about the dampness of a wrung sponge — water beads on your palm but doesn't run. Too wet is the single most common killer at this stage. The roots you're trying to grow are adventitious, oxygen-hungry, and will drown in saturated moss faster than they would in straight water (where at least the surface exchanges gas).

Pot loosely in a clear plastic cup or nursery pot with drainage. Clear lets you monitor root initiation without disturbing the plant. Bury the node or rhizome shallowly — half-exposed is fine for _Philodendron_ and most _Anthurium_; the goal is contact, not burial. Some growers swear by perlite-only or pon for acclimation, and they aren't wrong, but sphagnum forgives more beginner mistakes and rehydrates dehydrated tissue faster.

sections.heading: The chamber: humidity without stagnation
paragraphs: A freshly imported aroid has been sealed in a humid box for four to ten days. Its stomata are wide open, its cuticle is thin, and if you put it directly onto a shelf at 45% household humidity, the leaves will crisp within 48 hours. The chamber bridges that gap. A clear 66-quart tote with the lid cracked an inch, a IKEA Fabrikör cabinet, a converted Detolf — anything that holds 80–90% RH with some air movement works.

Air movement is the part people skip. A small clip fan on the lowest setting, aimed at the chamber wall rather than the plants, prevents the still, saturated micro-pockets where _Erwinia_ and _Pseudomonas_ throw parties. You want the leaves to flutter occasionally, not dance. If you see condensation pooling on leaf surfaces for hours at a time, increase airflow or decrease humidity by five points.

Light should be modest for the first two weeks: 80–120 µmol/m²/s at the leaf, roughly what a north window gives in summer, or a dimmable LED bar run at 30%. The plant cannot photosynthesize meaningfully without roots, and excess light just accelerates water loss through leaves it can't replace. Bump light up gradually as roots emerge.

sections.heading: The humidity ramp
paragraphs: After two to three weeks — once you can see new root tips pushing through the moss against the cup wall — start the ramp. The goal is to move the plant from 90% RH to whatever your growing space actually holds, over roughly three to four weeks. Drop the chamber humidity by about five percentage points per week by widening the lid gap, then by moving the plant to a more open shelf, then finally to ambient.

Watch the newest leaf, not the old ones. The leaf that hardened off in a Sumatran nursery is never going to look right in your apartment; expect it to yellow or abscise eventually and don't grieve it. The leaf the plant pushes for you, under your light and your humidity, is the one that tells you whether acclimation worked. If it emerges full-sized and unblemished, you've done it.

Velvet-leaved species — _Anthurium magnificum_, _crystallinum_, _papillilaminum_, _forgetii_ — need the slowest ramp and the highest final humidity, ideally 70%+ long-term. Thicker-cuticled climbers like [_Philodendron gloriosum_](/the-leaf/philodendron-gloriosum) or _verrucosum_ tolerate 55–60% once established. _Spiritus-sancti_ is famously fussy about airflow and will spot if kept wet and still, but it acclimates to surprisingly low humidity once rooted.

sections.heading: Root recovery and the temptation to fertilize
paragraphs: Do not fertilize for the first four weeks. The plant has no roots capable of regulated uptake, and salts in the moss will burn the very tissue you're trying to grow. After you see active white root tips an inch or longer, begin with a quarter-strength balanced fertilizer — something around 100–150 ppm N — applied to already-damp moss, never to dry media.

Bottom heat helps more than people admit. A seedling mat under the chamber, set to maintain 75–78°F at the root zone, can cut rooting time roughly in half for _Anthurium_ and velvet _Philodendron_. Above 82°F you start cooking beneficial microbes and encouraging pathogens; a cheap thermostat probe is worth twenty dollars.

If a cutting hasn't initiated roots after six weeks, unpot it and look. Sometimes the node is callusing but stalled; a fresh cut just below the callus and a return to fresh moss restarts the process. Sometimes there's quiet rot you couldn't see. Better to intervene at week six than to find a hollow petiole at week ten.

sections.heading: What the first sixty days actually look like
paragraphs: Week one: the plant looks worse than it did in the seller's photos. This is normal. Old leaves may yellow or drop. Resist the urge to do anything except maintain conditions.

Weeks two to four: root initiation, if it's going to happen, happens here. You'll see white nubs against the cup wall, then thin exploratory roots, then branching. The oldest leaf may abscise. A new leaf may start to push from the growth point — usually a good sign, sometimes a stress response, hard to tell which until it opens.

Weeks five to eight: the humidity ramp, the first cautious feeding, the first new leaf hardening off under your conditions. By day sixty, a successful acclimation looks like a plant with a working root system, one new leaf that belongs to your space, and the old import leaves either retained or cleanly shed. The plant is now yours in a biological sense, not just a financial one. The next leaf is the one you grew.
